column1: What does an LLM output when predicting the next token in a sequence?
column2: A probability distribution over every token in its vocabulary.
column3: This is why it's called a "language model" — it models the distribution of language.

column1: How does an LLM convert the probability distribution into the next output token?
column2: It samples from the distribution rather than always picking the highest-probability token.
column3: Greedy decoding = always pick max. Sampling = roll the dice.

column1: Why can the same prompt produce different outputs from an LLM?
column2: Because the LLM samples from the probability distribution over next tokens, introducing randomness into the selection.
column3: Temperature controls this randomness. Higher temp = more uniform distribution.

column1: What does "causal" mean when describing next-word prediction training?
column2: The prediction at position N depends only on positions 1 through N-1 — it cannot use future context.
column3: This is why it's also called "autoregressive" — auto (self) + regressive (looking backward).

column1: Why does next-word prediction's causal structure make it better for generation than fill-in-the-middle?
column2: Generation must happen left-to-right, one token at a time. Causal training mirrors this. Fill-in-the-middle sees both sides so it cannot start from scratch.
column3: BERT uses masked prediction and excels at understanding tasks but cannot generate coherent text.

column1: Why does next-word prediction give more training signal from the same data?
column2: Every token becomes a training example (given tokens 1..N, predict N+1). Masked prediction only trains on the ~15% of positions that are masked.
column3: For a 100-token sentence: next-word gives 99 training pairs. Masked gives ~15.

column1: What specific mechanism is the transformer architecture built around?
column2: Self-attention — each token computes relevance scores against every other token in the sequence.
column3: The paper is titled "Attention is All You Need".

column1: How does a transformer process a sequence differently from an RNN?
column2: RNNs step through tokens one at a time. Transformers process the entire sequence in one parallel pass.
column3: This is why transformers can handle much longer contexts than RNNs.

column1: What problem did the transformer's parallelism solve?
column2: It made training on massive datasets feasible — GPUs could process all tokens simultaneously instead of stepping one by one.
column3: GPT-3 trained on 300B tokens. That scale was impossible with RNNs.

column1: What architectural family did transformers replace for language modeling?
column2: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which processed tokens sequentially and struggled with long-range dependencies due to vanishing gradients.

column1: Where does the label for position N come from in language model pretraining?
column2: The label is simply the token at position N+1 in the training text.
column3: the cat sat on the → model predicts "mat" which is already in the text.

column1: Why is language model pretraining called "self-supervised"?
column2: The text itself generates the supervision signal because each token serves as the label for the preceding tokens.
column3: Contrast with supervised learning where humans must annotate data.

column1: What is the concrete relationship between input and label in autoregressive LM pretraining?
column2: The input is tokens 1 through N and the label is token N+1 from the same sequence.
column3: No separate labeled dataset is created; the sentence contains both input and target.

column1: How does the source of labels differ between supervised and self-supervised learning?
column2: In supervised learning labels come from external human annotation; in self-supervised learning labels are derived from the data's own structure.
column3: Supervised: human labels "spam/not spam". Self-supervised: input sequence itself provides the target.

column1: What does "self" in "self-supervised learning" actually refer to?
column2: The data supervising itself using patterns in its own structure — not the model training itself.
column3: Common trap: "self" means the model self-corrects. Reality: the data generates its own labels.

column1: Why is next-word prediction classified as self-supervised?
column2: Because the corpus itself supplies the targets — the next word is the label, no human annotation needed.
column3: The cat sat on the ___ → model predicts "mat" from context in the same unmodified text.

column1: How does the output space of classification fine-tuning differ from instruction fine-tuning?
column2: Classification collapses to a fixed set of category labels; instruction preserves full natural language generation.
column3: Example: classification → "positive" from {positive, negative}, instruction → "three bullet points: ..."

column1: What constrains the output vocabulary of a classification fine-tuned model?
column2: Only the category labels seen during fine-tuning are possible outputs; the model cannot produce labels outside those classes.
column3: If trained on {positive, negative, neutral}, it will never output "mixed".

column1: What capability does instruction fine-tuning add to a base language model?
column2: It enables the model to follow natural language instructions and produce natural language responses rather than merely completing text.
column3: This is how ChatGPT was made from GPT-3 — instruction fine-tuning on instruction-response pairs.

column1: GPT-2 and GPT-3 are both from OpenAI — why is GPT-2 not a "foundation model" for GPT-3?
column2: They were separately pretrained from scratch at different scales, not fine-tuned from each other.
column3: Foundation model paradigm: one base model fine-tuned for many tasks.

column1: What is the actual relationship between GPT-2 and GPT-3?
column2: Independent pretraining runs — GPT-3 was not built by fine-tuning GPT-2; each was pretrained from scratch at larger scale.
column3: Even though GPT-3 came after GPT-2, it did not use GPT-2's weights as a starting point.

column1: What is ChatGPT under the hood?
column2: ChatGPT (2022) is GPT-3 fine-tuned on instruction-following data, not a separately pretrained model.
column3: InstructGPT was the direct predecessor. GPT-3.5-turbo is a different fine-tuned variant.

column1: What makes BERT a foundation model?
column2: It was pretrained once then fine-tuned for many separate downstream tasks without retraining the base each time.
column3: This "pretrain then fine-tune" paradigm defines foundation models — same base weights reused across tasks.

column1: What was the estimated cost of GPT-3 pretraining?
column2: ~$4.6 million in cloud compute.
column3: That scale explains why only large labs train from scratch.

column1: How many tokens was GPT-3 trained on?
column2: 300 billion tokens.
column3: About 10x the entire English Wikipedia per day of training.

column1: What two numbers did the user mix up about GPT-3?
column2: They confused the data volume (300B tokens) with the dollar cost (~$4.6M).
column3: They said "30 billion worth of data" — both the magnitude and concept were wrong.

column1: How does the encoder process a source sentence in transformer encoder-decoder models?
column2: Reads the entire input sequence in parallel, building a context-aware representation where each token incorporates information from all other tokens.
column3: e.g., in "The bank can fall", the encoder sees full context to encode "bank" as financial institution.

column1: Why is an encoder needed for machine translation?
column2: To disambiguate the source sentence by processing it all at once, producing a context-aware representation the decoder references.
column3: Without full-context encoding, ambiguous words like "bank" would lack the disambiguation needed for accurate translation.

column1: How does the decoder generate output tokens in an encoder-decoder architecture?
column2: One token at a time, left to right, attending to both the encoder's output and its own previously generated tokens.
column3: Generation is autoregressive — each step depends on the previous, making decoding inherently sequential.

column1: What are the two attention sources the decoder uses at each generation step?
column2: The encoder's output (cross-attention) for source context and its own previously generated tokens (self-attention) for output fluency.

column1: Why does translation require both an encoder and a decoder?
column2: The encoder handles full-source understanding and disambiguation while the decoder handles target-language text generation — neither alone can do both jobs.
column3: A decoder-only model can translate with prompting but lacks a dedicated module for pre-encoding source context.

column1: What architectural component does BERT use from the original transformer?
column2: BERT uses only the encoder half, which reads the entire input bidirectionally.
column3: GPT uses the decoder half — unidirectional, left-to-right only.

column1: How were BERT and GPT trained differently?
column2: BERT uses masked language modeling (predict randomly masked tokens using full context). GPT uses next-token prediction (predict next token using only left context).
column3: BERT: "The [MASK] sat on the mat" → "cat". GPT: "The cat sat" → "on".

column1: Given a sentiment analysis task, which model would you choose and why?
column2: BERT, because its bidirectional encoder architecture is optimized for understanding and classification tasks rather than generation.
column3: GPT's unidirectional decoder excels at autoregressive generation, not classification.

column1: In self-attention, what question does each token ask about every other token?
column2: Which other tokens in this sequence are most relevant to interpreting this token?

column1: What does self-attention determine about the word "it" in "The cat sat on the mat because it was tired"?
column2: It lets "it" attend strongly to "cat" and weakly to "mat" to resolve coreference.

column1: What three vectors is each token transformed into for self-attention?
column2: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V).

column1: How are attention scores computed between two tokens?
column2: By taking the dot product of one token's Query vector with the other token's Key vector.

column1: What forms the final output for a token after attention scores are computed?
column2: A weighted sum of all tokens' Value vectors, weighted by their normalized attention scores.

column1: Why does self-attention handle long-range dependencies better than RNNs?
column2: Information flows directly between any two positions without going through the chain of words between them.

column1: What does "autoregressive" mean in the context of language models?
column2: Each output token is fed back in as input to generate the next token.
column3: GPT generates "the" → feeds it back → generates "cat" → feeds "the cat" back → generates "sat".

column1: Why is autoregressive generation slow?
column2: Tokens must be generated one at a time because each step's output becomes input for the next — no parallelization possible at inference.

column1: Why can't an autoregressive model generate all tokens in parallel at inference?
column2: Each token depends causally on all previous tokens, so later tokens cannot exist before earlier ones.

column1: How many examples does the model receive in zero-shot vs few-shot prompting?
column2: Zero-shot gets no examples (task description only). Few-shot gets 2–5 examples demonstrating the pattern before the new case.
column3: GPT-3 notably improved zero-shot capability over GPT-2.

column1: Why is zero-shot considered harder than few-shot?
column2: The model must infer a completely novel task from a plain-language instruction with no examples to anchor its behaviour.

column1: Why does few-shot usually outperform zero-shot in practice?
column2: The examples in the prompt clarify the expected output format and pattern, reducing ambiguity for the model.

column1: What atomic unit does an LLM token represent after tokenization?
column2: A subword unit — a whole word, syllable, punctuation mark, or word fragment.
column3: Common words like "cat" are one token while "unbelievable" splits into "un", "believ", "able".

column1: How does an LLM handle common vs uncommon words during tokenization?
column2: Common words stay as one token; uncommon words get split into subword pieces from the fixed vocabulary.
column3: Rough rule: 1 token ≈ 0.75 English words.

column1: What is the approximate token-to-word ratio for English text in LLMs?
column2: About 1 token per 0.75 English words (or ~1.3 tokens per word).
column3: Spaces and punctuation also count as tokens.

column1: What practical limitation does an LLM's fixed vocabulary impose?
column2: Words not in the vocabulary get split into known subword pieces — no out-of-vocabulary tokens exist.
column3: GPT-4 has a fixed vocabulary of 50,257 tokens.

column1: What was the total number of tokens GPT-3 was trained on?
column2: ~300 billion tokens.
column3: CommonCrawl 410B (60%), WebText2 19B (22%), Books1 12B (8%), Books2 55B (8%), Wikipedia 3B (3%).

column1: How many tokens of Wikipedia were in GPT-3's training corpus?
column2: 3 billion tokens — not 3 million words as commonly misremembered.

column1: What percentage of GPT-3's training data came from CommonCrawl?
column2: 60% (410B tokens) — the largest source despite being the lowest quality per-token.

column1: Why is Wikipedia's 3% share notable in GPT-3's data mix?
column2: It shows how little high-quality curated text is needed relative to raw web data.
column3: Wikipedia was the smallest source by volume but highest quality.

column1: What two book corpora were in GPT-3's training data?
column2: Books1 (12B tokens) and Books2 (55B tokens), each at 8% of the total mix.

column1: What did the Chinchilla scaling laws conclude about data and parameters?
column2: For optimal performance, models should scale training data proportionally alongside parameters.

column1: Why did GPT-3's capabilities surprisingly exceed GPT-2's?
column2: GPT-3 trained on ~300B tokens vs GPT-2's ~1B — massive scale unlocked emergent capabilities.

column1: How does the benefit of additional training tokens change as total count grows?
column2: Past a threshold, each additional token provides diminishing returns rather than linear improvement.

column1: What is an emergent behavior in LLMs?
column2: A capability that wasn't explicitly trained for and doesn't appear in smaller models but suddenly appears at sufficient scale.
column3: GPT can translate and do arithmetic despite training only on next-word prediction.

column1: How did GPT-3's translation ability surprise researchers?
column2: It showed that capabilities thought to require specialized training could emerge spontaneously from next-word prediction alone at sufficient scale.

column1: What pattern of capability onset with model scaling surprised researchers?
column2: Capabilities switched on suddenly past a threshold rather than improving gradually — no clear mechanism explained the switch.

column1: How many transformer layers does GPT-3 have?
column2: 96 transformer layers.

column1: How many parameters does GPT-3 contain?
column2: 175 billion parameters.

column1: Approximately how much memory do GPT-3's weights consume in fp32?
column2: Roughly 350 GB.

column1: What was the estimated compute cost to pretrain GPT-3?
column2: Between $4-12 million (estimates vary).

column1: What was GPT-1's key contribution?
column2: First demonstrated that pretraining + fine-tuning worked effectively (117M params, 1B tokens).
column3: Released 2018.

column1: How did GPT-2 build on GPT-1?
column2: Showed that scaling parameters to 1.5B improved performance; OpenAI withheld the full model over misuse concerns.
column3: Released 2019.

column1: How many parameters did GPT-3 have and what emerged at that scale?
column2: 175B parameters (300B tokens) enabled strong few-shot and zero-shot abilities without fine-tuning.
column3: Released 2020. Base GPT-3 still could not follow instructions.

column1: What is the technical relationship between ChatGPT and GPT-3?
column2: ChatGPT is GPT-3.5 (a GPT-3 variant) fine-tuned on instruction data via InstructGPT — not a new base model.
column3: Released late 2022. Fine-tuning — not larger scale — enabled chat and instruction-following.

column1: What were the approximate parameter counts across GPT generations?
column2: 117M (GPT-1) → 1.5B (GPT-2) → 175B (GPT-3), roughly 10x or more each generation.

column1: What do you gain by starting from a pretrained model instead of training from scratch?
column2: You skip the ~$4.6M compute bill and get a model that already understands language, grammar, facts, and reasoning.

column1: What do you lose by starting from a pretrained model instead of training from scratch?
column2: You inherit the pretraining data's biases and are stuck with the architecture — you can't reshape the fundamental "brain".

column1: Why is fine-tuning faster and cheaper than training from scratch?
column2: The pretrained model already learned universal language patterns, so fine-tuning only adjusts later layers on a small dataset.
column3: Training from scratch learns everything from random initialization across billions of parameters.

column1: What did the Transformer paper replace to achieve its breakthrough?
column2: It replaced recurrence (sequential token processing from RNNs) entirely with self-attention.
column3: The paper is titled "Attention is All You Need".

column1: Why couldn't RNNs train efficiently on long sequences?
column2: Two problems: no parallelization (tokens processed one at a time) and vanishing gradients (information degraded across sequential steps).

column1: What two properties did self-attention give that recurrence could not?
column2: Full parallel processing across the sequence and direct connections between any two tokens regardless of distance.

column1: What happens if a model has no self-attention mechanism?
column2: Each token is processed in isolation with no way to query or aggregate information from other tokens — like a bag-of-words model.

column1: Why does "The spider that the cat that the dog chased ate was fat" become incomprehensible without self-attention?
column2: The model cannot resolve long-range subject-verb dependencies because it has no mechanism to connect distant tokens.

column1: Without self-attention, what happens to a token's representation of non-local context?
column2: It is lost — each token's representation contains only its own embedding with no information from other tokens.

column1: Can coherent text exist without genuine understanding?
column2: Yes — LLMs prove coherence and understanding are separable. They produce grammatically correct text without genuine grounding.
column3: Understanding requires world models and beliefs about truth, not just statistical pattern matching.

column1: What distinguishes coherent text from genuine understanding?
column2: Coherent text follows statistical word-sequence patterns. Understanding requires grounding in meaning and world models.

column1: Why do LLMs hallucinate despite generating coherent text?
column2: They model word-sequence statistics only with no grounding in meaning, world models, or beliefs about truth.

column1: What does genuine understanding require beyond statistical pattern matching?
column2: Grounding in meaning, maintaining world models, and forming beliefs about truth.
